lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Weather and Seasons in Mandarin for African Agribusiness

Weather vocabulary is not small talk in African agribusiness â it is working capital. A maize trader in Nakuru, a cocoa exporter in Kumasi, or a floriculture manager in Addis Ababa all need to ask a Mandarin-speaking counterpart about planting windows, cold-chain risk, or typhoon delays in a Chinese port. This lesson gives you the practical Mandarin you need to discuss weather, seasons, temperature, forecasts, and extreme weather in a business context. Every phrase here is chosen because it appears in real sourcing conversations, shipping updates, and supplier calls.

Chinese weather language is highly structured. Once you learn the pattern, you can generate hundreds of useful sentences. The core pattern is: place + weather + adjective, for example NÃ irÃ¨i xiÃ  yÇ (Nairobi rains). Temperature uses dÃ¹ (degrees), seasons use jÃ¬jiÃ©, and forecasts use yÃ¹bÃ o. Master these three anchors and you can negotiate delivery windows, ask about harvest conditions, and flag weather risk in a WeChat message within seconds.

Key Sentence Patterns for Business

Use these frames to build your own messages. Replace the bracketed items with your own context.

  • [Place] xiÃ  yÇ ma? â Does it rain in [place]? KÃ¹mÇxÄ« xiÃ  yÇ ma?
  • [Place] de wÄndÃ¹ shÃ¬ duÅshao? â What is the temperature in [place]?
  • XiÃ  zhÅu yÇu [weather] ma? â Will there be [weather] next week?
  • YÃ¹bÃ o shuÅ [weather] â The forecast says [weather].
  • WÇ zuÃ¬ xÇhuan [season] â I like [season] best.
  • [Weather] huÃ¬ yÇngxiÇng [business activity] â [Weather] will affect [business activity].
  • QÇng zhÃ¹yÃ¬ jÃ­duÄn tiÄnqÃ¬ jÇnggÃ o â Please note the extreme weather warning.

Small Talk That Opens Doors

In Chinese business culture, weather small talk is a relationship tool, not filler. A supplier in Guangzhou will warm up if you open with GuÇngzhÅu jÄ«ntiÄn hÄn rÃ¨ ba? (It's very hot in Guangzhou today, isn't it?). From there you can pivot to logistics, harvest timing, or price. Keep it to two or three exchanges, then move to business. Complimenting the weather in the supplier's city signals that you pay attention to their operating conditions â a subtle but powerful trust signal.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Extreme Weather and Force Majeure

Never ship perishable African agricultural goods (flowers, fresh produce, cocoa) without checking the Chinese destination forecast for tÃ¡ifÄng (typhoon), hÃ³ngshuÇ (flood), or gÄowÄn (heatwave). Chinese ports such as Shanghai, Ningbo, and Guangzhou can shut for 48â72 hours during typhoon warnings. Always confirm in writing: NÇmen nÃ r yÇu jÃ­duÄn tiÄnqÃ¬ jÇnggÃ o ma? (Do you have extreme weather warnings there?). If yes, invoke your force majeure clause before dispatch, not after. Losses from uninsured weather delays are the leading cause of payment disputes between African exporters and Chinese importers.
